name: Light Olive
lede: Light Olive is a descriptive name for a pale olive, and the books show it in an old color-chart skin description and as part of a paint name.

sections.title: Old charts, plain words
sections.body:
Werner's nomenclature, the nineteenth-century color chart used by naturalists, was applied to medicine, and Baty quotes a medical use of the chart in which a skin tone is hazel, wood brown, light olive or wax yellow [1]. Baty's paint-chart comparison table also includes a Light Olive Brown entry [2]. In Paterson, sallow is defined as a light olive green, and sage-grey as a greyish olive [3][4]. The name is a descriptive pair, light plus olive, rather than a named dye [1][3].

Neighbors in our names are [[olive]], [[sage-green]] and [[moss-green]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch matches 43 of 23,781 archive paintings (0.18%, as photographed), rarer than 58% of the named colors [5]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 0.8% of 1,674 paintings, 5.0 times the rate expected from the same museums [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 58% of the 26 paintings that hold it [5]. The earliest dated match is a painting by Lucas Cranach from 1548, though early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.
